label: the dry run (Claude Haiku 5.5 as the player)

screens:
The session begins.

The city is behind you now, only a smudge of smoke to the north. To the west the Sea of Swords has gone the colour of old pewter, and the sun is sliding toward it. Tamsin walks a half-step ahead with your pack hitched high on her shoulders, talking about who on the quay owes whom, and the cat pads along the verge, tail up, stopping now and then to smell the gorse.

Then the road bends around a stand of wind-bent pines, and there is a wagon.

It is a small two-wheeled carter's cart, tipped at an angle, one wheel sunk in the ditch. The mule is still in harness. It lifts its head, looks at you without much interest, and goes back to the grass. Sacks are lashed down under a canvas. Nobody is on the seat, nobody is in the ditch, nobody is on the road as far as you can see, and beyond the bend the road can't be seen at all. Something small and pale lies on the seat, too far away to make out.

Tamsin stops. The cat has stopped too, ears forward, staring at the trees.

"Well," Tamsin says, already shrugging the pack a little lower, "nobody leaves a mule standing. Not on this road." She looks back at you. The light is going. The Friendly Arm is still somewhere ahead.

Party: Tamsin (HP 11/11) — A porter from the Baldur's Gate quay who has carried James's pack since the evening he arrived. She knows the quay and everyone on it, and she is reckless. She 
Place: The Coast Way, south of Baldur's Gate
Time: Day 1 · afternoon

James closes a hand on Tamsin's arm. She stops talking mid-word, which for her is something.

"Down it is," she murmurs. She lowers the pack into the gorse at the roadside and stays crouched beside it with one strap looped round her wrist. After a moment she picks up a stone about the size of her fist and holds it the way quay people do. "Carters don't walk off from a full load. Not even drunk ones, and I've seen plenty of drunk ones."

The cat goes without a sound. It drops low along the verge, belly to the grass, and slips in under the pines. Through the bond the smells reach James the way they reach the cat, more as a feeling than as words:

*Resin. Needles, crushed. Many. Sweat, big ones, not long gone. Iron, oiled. Smoke, green wood, far, that way.* There is a pause while it noses at something. *Small one. Afraid. Went with them.*

James walks on along the far edge of the road, slow and in plain sight, a traveller with his hand near his hip. Reading the ground is old scout's work and he barely has to look for it. The cart's wheel ruts come up from the south, swing round in a wide turn, and end in the ditch. The cart didn't slide in. Somebody put it there. The verge is churned by heavy boots: four pairs, maybe five, and one set broader and deeper than the rest. Between them runs a smaller set of hobnailed prints, scuffing, as if the man wearing them had been walked along. All of it heads back south, round the bend. There's no blood anywhere, on the road, the cart or the grass.

Close up, the mule's lead turns out to be knotted to the shaft. The knot is loose, with enough slack to let it graze. The mule lifts its head at James's question, chews on it, and pushes its nose into his sleeve in case there's an apple in there. There isn't. It goes back to the grass.

From beyond the bend comes the sound of water running over stones. Then a voice, deep, says one word that isn't Common, and a second voice answers with a short bark of a laugh. After that it's quiet. A thin grey thread of smoke goes up above the pines to the south, and the sun is touching the sea.

On the cart seat, close enough now to see properly, is a flat piece of bone about the length of a hand. It's pale and has been scratched all over with marks that look like letters. Someone has set a pebble on it so the wind won't carry it off.

James keeps his voice low. "Tamsin. Stay with the pack and the mule. If a carter comes running out of the trees, you're a porter waiting for her master, and you don't know anything."

"Waiting for my master, who's late and owes me," Tamsin says. "Easy. I've done that one for real." She moves over beside the mule and stays crouched, stone in hand. The mule ignores her.

James wraps the bone in the cloth from his pack and lifts it by the edge, tilting it toward the last of the light. You were right that some of the marks are counting strokes. Along the bottom are ten gates, each four upright strokes with a fifth drawn across them, the way a quartermaster counts sacks, and after them a rough circle. Above the count, though, the marks are letters. They're in Common, cut by someone who had to work at it, every letter drawn separately and some of them backwards:

**ODO FENIK — SALT**

and under the gates, more deeply cut than the rest:

**WYRM ROCK — LT**

James slides the bone back under its pebble exactly as it was and crouches by the wheel.

The cat is low in the pines with its tail flat. It listens to what he tells it, and then it goes, down toward the sound of the water. The trees are thickest on that side.

Pip gets there unseen. It slips between the alder roots along the bank, and the sound of the water covers what little noise a cat makes. For a while its feelings keep coming through the bond, *wet stones, cold, smoke stronger*. Then they fade the way a voice does down a long corridor, and the bond goes quiet.

*(The familiar's bond carries words only within 100 feet. Beyond that it stays silent unless you take its senses, and while you do, you're blind and deaf where you are.)*

James waits. A gull goes over. The mule tears up grass. The sun sinks halfway into the sea and the shadows of the pines reach across the road.

Then the cat is back. It comes out of the gorse at his knee with its fur damp, and it pushes against his boot once before the feelings start coming again:

*Stone road over water. Bridge.* A picture comes with it: a low humped stone bridge some fifty paces past the bend, and a fire on the near bank under it, built of green wood that smokes badly. *Three. Two by fire, eating. One up on the stones, watching the road, this way.* The watcher is a picture in grey, broad, with something long over its shoulder. *Bow smell. Gut string.*

*Not the big one. Big one went in.* Pip turns its head east toward the dark wood across the road. *Big one, one more, and the small one. Trees, that way. Trail.*

Then the part James asked about. *Small one: rope smell. Hands, near. No blood. Walked on his own feet, slow. Afraid. Tired.* After a moment comes something smaller and stranger. *Under the bridge, at the end. Earth dug, not new, not old. Stones put back.*

The cat sits down against his boot, tail wrapped round its feet, and won't look at the bend.

Two voices are still talking quietly by the fire. One of them laughs again. The light has about half an hour left.

 The cat never got close to being seen. It crept along the stream bank under the thickest alders to within a few yards of the fire and back again, and none of the three by the bridge looked its way. The archer kept watching the empty road to the north, and the two eating kept on talking with their backs to the water.

James stays low behind the tipped cart, with the canvas and the sacks between him and the bend. Tamsin nods at the instruction about the mule and says nothing, which for her is twice in one evening.

He puts his hand on the cat's back. Under his palm it's warm and still damp. Pip listens to the whole order with its ears flat. Then it slides out from under his hand and goes back the way it came, down into the gorse and toward the alders and the water.

Through the bond the cat's feelings come thin and steady: *wet, cold, smoke*. Then they fade, the same as last time, past the point where the bond carries words.

James lifts the crossbow out of the gorse and keeps it low behind the wheel. He runs a thumb along the string. It's dry and tight, and the tiller shows no crack. He keeps his thumb well clear of the nut and does nothing that would click. Then he lays the crossbow across his knees and leaves the rapier where it is.

He leans toward Tamsin and speaks very low. "The one under the stones is dead. Don't look at the bridge when you walk back."

Tamsin's hand tightens on her stone. For a moment she doesn't talk at all. Then the words come out quick and flat, the way they do when she wants them over with. "Right. Not looking. Walked past a man face-down in the harbour once and never turned my head. The watch thanked me for it." She looks at the mule, then at the sacks under the canvas. "Somebody's waiting on this salt, then, and it isn't coming."

The sun is down to a red rim on the water. The pines' shadows have crossed the road and started up the far verge.

After a while the bond warms again, faint at first and then clear. Pip comes out of the gorse at his knee. It's wetter than before and has a burr stuck in its ruff. It presses against his boot and reports:

*Under the bridge, water side. Close. Not seen.*

*Small one: not here. No rope by fire. No stake.* There's a picture of the fire, the two big shapes, scraps of bone and gristle, and nothing else. *Rope smell goes that way.* Pip's attention swings east toward the dark wood across the road. *With big one. Old trail, not new.*

*Awake: three. All three.* The two by the fire are still eating. One has stretched out on his elbow with his boots toward the water.

Then the watcher. Pip shows him in grey from below, a broad back against the paling sky. *Bow on back, not in hands. Looks north, road. Turns head: down, to fire, when they laugh. Then north again.* There's a pause, and something Pip noticed on its own: *Turns head east too. Trees. Often.* It shows him twice more, chin lifting toward the wood across the road and holding there, the way a man looks along a road for someone who's late.

The cat sits down against James's boot and licks the stream off one paw.

 *(Out of game: James never declared the Eldritch Blast. He only said he'd rather use it than the crossbow if it came to that, so nobody has been attacked and no fight has started. The other three, checking the crossbow, leaving the rapier on his hip and what he told Tamsin, all happened in the story last turn and didn't need a roll.)*

messages.text:
I stop Tamsin with a hand on her arm and keep my voice low. "Hold here a moment. Set the pack down where you can grab it."

I watch the trees for a few breaths before I say anything else. "Nobody leaves a mule standing, you said. Somebody's usually still nearby when that happens, and they're not usually in a hurry to show themselves." I glance at the cat. "Go on, then. Along the verge, into the pines. Stay low and tell me what you smell."

Then I start toward the cart, slowly, keeping the road between the ditch and me, with my hand near the rapier at my hip and my eyes on the shadows under the trees. I don't reach for the crossbow yet. If something is waiting in the pines, I want it to see a traveller and not a man ready to fight.

"Mule," I say quietly, to the animal more than to Tamsin. "Who did this to you?"

"Tamsin, stay with the pack and the mule. If a carter comes running out of the trees, you're a porter waiting for her master, and you don't know anything." I take the bone off the seat by its edge, using the cloth from my pack so I don't touch the scratches, and turn it toward the light. The marks are short and grouped in strokes of five, the way a quartermaster counts sacks. Some of the groups are crossed through. I slide it back under its pebble exactly as I found it.

I crouch by the wheel and look at Pip, sitting low in the pines with its tail flat. "Pip. Go closer, along the stream side where the trees are thickest. Find where they're sitting and count them. Find the small one, and tell me whether it's tied, hurt, or just frightened. Don't let anyone see you, and come back the moment someone looks your way."

Then I wait, keeping my back to the cart and my eyes on the bend, my hand near the rapier and the crossbow lying loaded in the gorse beside my pack. I don't move toward the water until the cat has either found something or been seen.

I keep the cart between me and the bridge while I think. Half an hour of light, three of them at the fire, one with a bow. The cart's carter is under the stones, and the small one is alive and roped. I'm not going to walk down the road in the open.

"Tamsin, when I say, you take the mule back to the bend and tie it where the pines hide it. Don't come after me unless you hear me shout your name."

Then I crouch, put my hand on the cat's back, and reach for the bond.

"Pip. Go back under the bridge, on the water side. The small one's rope. Is it tied to a stake, or to a hand? Is there a second rope? Count any that stay awake, and tell me which way the bow is pointing when the watcher turns his head. Then come back the same way. Don't cross the open ground, and don't let the water make you careless."

While the cat is gone, I take the crossbow out of the gorse and check the string without loading it. I don't want the click to carry to the bridge. Eldritch Blast is quieter than a bolt, and at this range I'd rather be close to the archer than trust the crossbow. I leave the rapier on my hip. If it comes to a close fight, I'll already have failed.

I tell Tamsin, very low: "The one under the stones is dead. Don't look at the bridge when you walk back."

**What worked:** The scene felt like a road in the Sword Coast. The wrong details (the loose mule knot, the stone on the bone tally, the boot prints heading back south) made me want to read the ground instead of just rolling for it. The cat scouting was the best part. Pip's reports came through as smells and pictures, and I could act on them without the GM having to spell everything out. Tamsin's voice was distinct and funny without being a joke, and the fading sun gave the choices a deadline.

**What broke:** The out-of-game blocks were too heavy. Each turn came with a full records dump, a list of "New person" and "New place" entries, and a roll log, and they were longer than the story they followed. Some of it leaked into the fiction in ways that were confusing: "Quest: Odo Fennick" appeared in the note as if I had accepted something I hadn't. The out-of-game note explaining that I hadn't declared Eldritch Blast was useful, but it should have been a single sentence. I also couldn't tell which numbers were mine. Pip's Stealth rolls appeared, but none of mine did, so I had no sense of whether my own checks were being made.

**What was missing:** Two turns in a row I only observed, through the cat, while the cat did the work. That is fine for a scouting beat, but I had no check of my own and nothing I was clearly good at. Sneaking up on the bridge, talking to the archer, or bluffing Tamsin's way past would each have used my skills (Deception +7, Persuasion +7), and none of them came up. Next time I'd like one moment where James's own talents are the answer, and where the roll that decides it is mine.

Yes. When Pip came back and reported the fire, the archer, and the broken stones under the bridge, I wanted to go down to the bridge myself and look at the grave. I wanted to see whether the stones were as Pip described and whether there was anything in the dirt, and to know the small one was alive with my own eyes.

I held back because the cat had just found a way past the fire unseen, and I was afraid that moving on the bank would wake the watcher. The cat had also reported that the archer turns his head toward the eastern trees, and I didn't know what was there. So I stayed behind the cart and let Pip keep going.

I also wanted to try talking to the archer as a soldier, using my old rank and the Tethyrian habit of giving orders. That would have used Intimidation or Deception, and my own roll would have decided it. I didn't get the chance, because the scene never gave me a moment where a stranger was close enough to address. That's the thing I missed most: a roll that was mine, on a problem I could have solved with my mouth.

turns.message:
I keep the cart between me and the bridge while I think. Half an hour of light, three of them at the fire, one with a bow. The cart's carter is under the stones, and the small one is alive and roped. I'm not going to walk down the road in the open.

"Tamsin, when I say, you take the mule back to the bend and tie it where the pines hide it. Don't come after me unless you hear me shout your name."

Then I crouch, put my hand on the cat's back, and reach for the bond.

"Pip. Go back under the bridge, on the water side. The small one's rope. Is it tied to a stake, or to a hand? Is there a second rope? Count any that stay awake, and tell me which way the bow is pointing when the watcher turns his head. Then come back the same way. Don't cross the open ground, and don't let the water make you careless."

While the cat is gone, I take the crossbow out of the gorse and check the string without loading it. I don't want the click to carry to the bridge. Eldritch Blast is quieter than a bolt, and at this range I'd rather be close to the archer than trust the crossbow. I leave the rapier on my hip. If it comes to a close fight, I'll already have failed.

I tell Tamsin, very low: "The one under the stones is dead. Don't look at the bridge when you walk back."
turns.reply:
James stays low behind the tipped cart, with the canvas and the sacks between him and the bend. Tamsin nods at the instruction about the mule and says nothing, which for her is twice in one evening.

He puts his hand on the cat's back. Under his palm it's warm and still damp. Pip listens to the whole order with its ears flat. Then it slides out from under his hand and goes back the way it came, down into the gorse and toward the alders and the water.

Through the bond the cat's feelings come thin and steady: *wet, cold, smoke*. Then they fade, the same as last time, past the point where the bond carries words.

James lifts the crossbow out of the gorse and keeps it low behind the wheel. He runs a thumb along the string. It's dry and tight, and the tiller shows no crack. He keeps his thumb well clear of the nut and does nothing that would click. Then he lays the crossbow across his knees and leaves the rapier where it is.

He leans toward Tamsin and speaks very low. "The one under the stones is dead. Don't look at the bridge when you walk back."

Tamsin's hand tightens on her stone. For a moment she doesn't talk at all. Then the words come out quick and flat, the way they do when she wants them over with. "Right. Not looking. Walked past a man face-down in the harbour once and never turned my head. The watch thanked me for it." She looks at the mule, then at the sacks under the canvas. "Somebody's waiting on this salt, then, and it isn't coming."

The sun is down to a red rim on the water. The pines' shadows have crossed the road and started up the far verge.

After a while the bond warms again, faint at first and then clear. Pip comes out of the gorse at his knee. It's wetter than before and has a burr stuck in its ruff. It presses against his boot and reports:

*Under the bridge, water side. Close. Not seen.*

*Small one: not here. No rope by fire. No stake.* There's a picture of the fire, the two big shapes, scraps of bone and gristle, and nothing else. *Rope smell goes that way.* Pip's attention swings east toward the dark wood across the road. *With big one. Old trail, not new.*

*Awake: three. All three.* The two by the fire are still eating. One has stretched out on his elbow with his boots toward the water.

Then the watcher. Pip shows him in grey from below, a broad back against the paling sky. *Bow on back, not in hands. Looks north, road. Turns head: down, to fire, when they laugh. Then north again.* There's a pause, and something Pip noticed on its own: *Turns head east too. Trees. Often.* It shows him twice more, chin lifting toward the wood across the road and holding there, the way a man looks along a road for someone who's late.

The cat sits down against James's boot and licks the stream off one paw.

 *(Out of game: James never declared the Eldritch Blast. He only said he'd rather use it than the crossbow if it came to that, so nobody has been attacked and no fight has started. The other three, checking the crossbow, leaving the rapier on his hip and what he told Tamsin, all happened in the story last turn and didn't need a roll.)*

note.text:
**What worked:** The scene felt like a road in the Sword Coast. The wrong details (the loose mule knot, the stone on the bone tally, the boot prints heading back south) made me want to read the ground instead of just rolling for it. The cat scouting was the best part. Pip's reports came through as smells and pictures, and I could act on them without the GM having to spell everything out. Tamsin's voice was distinct and funny without being a joke, and the fading sun gave the choices a deadline.

**What broke:** The out-of-game blocks were too heavy. Each turn came with a full records dump, a list of "New person" and "New place" entries, and a roll log, and they were longer than the story they followed. Some of it leaked into the fiction in ways that were confusing: "Quest: Odo Fennick" appeared in the note as if I had accepted something I hadn't. The out-of-game note explaining that I hadn't declared Eldritch Blast was useful, but it should have been a single sentence. I also couldn't tell which numbers were mine. Pip's Stealth rolls appeared, but none of mine did, so I had no sense of whether my own checks were being made.

**What was missing:** Two turns in a row I only observed, through the cat, while the cat did the work. That is fine for a scouting beat, but I had no check of my own and nothing I was clearly good at. Sneaking up on the bridge, talking to the archer, or bluffing Tamsin's way past would each have used my skills (Deception +7, Persuasion +7), and none of them came up. Next time I'd like one moment where James's own talents are the answer, and where the roll that decides it is mine.

after.text:
Yes. When Pip came back and reported the fire, the archer, and the broken stones under the bridge, I wanted to go down to the bridge myself and look at the grave. I wanted to see whether the stones were as Pip described and whether there was anything in the dirt, and to know the small one was alive with my own eyes.

I held back because the cat had just found a way past the fire unseen, and I was afraid that moving on the bank would wake the watcher. The cat had also reported that the archer turns his head toward the eastern trees, and I didn't know what was there. So I stayed behind the cart and let Pip keep going.

I also wanted to try talking to the archer as a soldier, using my old rank and the Tethyrian habit of giving orders. That would have used Intimidation or Deception, and my own roll would have decided it. I didn't get the chance, because the scene never gave me a moment where a stranger was close enough to address. That's the thing I missed most: a roll that was mine, on a problem I could have solved with my mouth.

opening.text:
The city is behind you now, only a smudge of smoke to the north. To the west the Sea of Swords has gone the colour of old pewter, and the sun is sliding toward it. Tamsin walks a half-step ahead with your pack hitched high on her shoulders, talking about who on the quay owes whom, and the cat pads along the verge, tail up, stopping now and then to smell the gorse.

Then the road bends around a stand of wind-bent pines, and there is a wagon.

It is a small two-wheeled carter's cart, tipped at an angle, one wheel sunk in the ditch. The mule is still in harness. It lifts its head, looks at you without much interest, and goes back to the grass. Sacks are lashed down under a canvas. Nobody is on the seat, nobody is in the ditch, nobody is on the road as far as you can see, and beyond the bend the road can't be seen at all. Something small and pale lies on the seat, too far away to make out.

Tamsin stops. The cat has stopped too, ears forward, staring at the trees.

"Well," Tamsin says, already shrugging the pack a little lower, "nobody leaves a mule standing. Not on this road." She looks back at you. The light is going. The Friendly Arm is still somewhere ahead.
